Another one from the Scott Adams "Persuasion Reading List", and pretty damn good.

Non-academic books on specialist subjects have a tricky balance to find. On one hand they have to be academically (if not scientifically) credible in that they have to set out the principles involved, but they also have to be readable enough that the average magazine reader doesn't get bored. Cialdini mostly gets this balance right. It might be the subject material (when you get down to it, most of the areas of persuasion and influence he talks about are quasi-biological, behavioural processes) or it might be Cialdini's chatty prose, but this book sets out a serious number of essential principles and combines them with a number of real world and surprising, even contrarian, examples of how and why those principles work.

One example: ever wondered why corporations would waste time and money doing those "write in" competitions, i.e. where you get invited to describe in 100 words or less why Churned-Up-Cat Dog Food is your dog food of choice in order to win a holiday to some slave-wages third world tropical island? The psychological trick they're playing on you is the same one the Chinese did to break the minds of American POWs captured in Korea. The Chinese would request POWs write out statements critical of the US regime. Sometimes they'd offer small inducements to the prisoners to do so.

After publicising these documents to their fellow prisoners, and more widely, a funny thing happened: the prisoners began to believe their written statements -- and more significantly, still believed in them after they were released from custody. There is a behavioural mechanism humans seem to have adapted: when we write a promise or a statement down, we will generally alter our behaviour to act in compliance with that statement, even if we did not believe it at the time. It seems that psychologically, while we can "forget" that we made an oral promise or statement, we find it much, much harder as human beings to pretend to forget or put aside previous written statements that we have made and, ideally, signed.

This is why the company wants you to write, in 100 words or less, why their dog food is great: they don't want your text for their advertising, they want you to write things like "This dog food is great because my dog really likes it" ... because there's a decent chance you'll actually believe it and keep buying Churned-Up-Cat, well after the contest is over. It is essentially a way of potentially pulling in hundreds of thousands of individual consumers on their own greed. It is the same reason door-to-door salesmen often make you fill out the form applying for whatever shitty product they are spruiking: what we write down, and in particular, what we write down and make public knowledge, we are psychologically keyed to live up to.

More positively, it is the real mechanism behind the old wise saw that "If you want to succeed at your goals, write them down."

This was one of the big head-exploding moments I had while reading the book. There are others: everything from Watergate to Kitty Genovese to Jonestown are covered in this book from the perspective of persuasion and influence, and there is not much I found incredible or (ha ha) not persuasive.

That said: it's probably one of those books you only read twice. Once for the experience and the surprises in his anecdotes, the second time to summarise the book's key points into a document for later use (which I did. 6 pages.) It doesn't contain complicated or very in-depth discussions on how to use these principles or how to avoid them being used against you, but then, it's not a true marketing book anyway. It's far more designed to help you recognise the tactics of "compliance professionals" and stop them being used against you. On the other hand, I do regard it as damn near essential reading in our modern age. One of Cialdini's more sobering insights is this: as life gets more and more complex, human beings are more and more likely to fall back on "shortcuts" to making decisions, which these influence levers are meant to hijack. That being so, my feeling is that the technological human - which we all are - will get more gullible as a species, not less. This is an important book to read and absorb at least once.

We had picked out multiple satellites zipping around and unfocusing your eyes you could easily see three at a time. Finally the first light started to peek above the horizon and I remember it vividly like a ball of plasma (most of my memories of sunrises aren't nearly so vivid). So there's this huge contrast of empty space and a sliver of molten yellow and we start tracking another seemingly larger satellite heading right towards the rising sun. Its trajectory seemed to shallow out and run nearly parallel to the horizon. Then it caught the light of the sun and lit up like a ball of fire in the sky. I thought I was witnessing a satellite in orbit in the perfect position to reflect first light right into our eyeballs. But I will never forget what happened next. It SLOWED DOWN once it was directly inside the sunrise and instead of passing over the horizon it leveled out and passed behind the trees, still reflecting all that light. What was probably 10-15 seconds felt like an eternity watching it sail above and then behind the trees. After it was gone I looked at my dad and asked "What was that?" and he kept staring at the sky, then said "Were not catching anything, lets go back."
